entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Djamila (also Jamila) was a preeminent *qiyan* (slave entertainer and courtesan) in Medina during the early 8th century CE, dying around 720 CE. Her unparalleled mastery of *ghina'* (vocal music and poetry) established her as a foundational figure in early Islamic music, profoundly influencing generations of musicians and poets across the burgeoning Arab empire. Djamila transcended her status as an enslaved woman through sheer artistic excellence, becoming a cultural icon whose salon attracted caliphs, princes, and leading intellectual figures of her time, thereby shaping the nascent courtly culture of the Islamic Golden Age. Her celebrated salon served as a crucial site for the development and transmission of sophisticated musical forms, bridging pre-Islamic Arabian traditions with the cosmopolitan influences of the rapidly expanding Islamic world.

Djamila's repertoire was vast, encompassing hundreds, if not thousands, of songs drawn from classical Arabic poetry and contemporary compositions. She was renowned for her innovative vocal techniques and her ability to perform *ghina'* with profound emotional depth and technical brilliance. Accounts from al-Isfahani's monumental *Kitāb al-Aghānī* (Book of Songs), compiled in the 10th century, detail her extensive travels, including a famous pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca accompanied by 50 female slave singers, all meticulously trained by her. This impressive entourage showcased her pedagogical influence and the widespread recognition of her artistic prowess. Her performances at the courts of figures like Caliph al-Walid I further solidified her status, demonstrating the integration of high-level musical entertainment into the highest echelons of Umayyad society.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Djamila's innovative vocal artistry and pedagogical influence fundamentally shaped early Islamic music, establishing a Medinan school that propagated across the nascent caliphate. Her life offers a crucial insight into the artistic and social mobility of talented enslaved women in the 8th century, challenging conventional historical narratives.
